Abena Bonsu, 43-year-old woman with hypertension and asthma, nut allergy, and no reported regular medications, presented on 03/01/26 with two weeks of progressive exertional breathlessness. She was tachycardic, tachypnoeic, borderline hypotensive, and hypoxic (SpO₂ 89–90% on room air), requiring low-flow oxygen, with improvement to approximately 92% on 2 L nasal cannula. Examination showed raised JVP, basal crepitations, mild hepatomegaly, and later a loud P2. ABG showed mild hypoxia (PaO₂ 8.5 kPa) with respiratory alkalosis. NT-proBNP was elevated (3,200–4,500 pg/mL), and D-dimer was elevated. Chest X-ray showed bilateral pulmonary congestion without focal consolidation or pneumothorax. She was admitted to the Respiratory HDU for suspected chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).

Therapeutic anticoagulation was initially planned with enoxaparin, followed by a plan for apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily while continuing LMWH until established. CTPA and echocardiography were requested. Physiotherapy began with diaphragmatic breathing exercises and light mobilisation.

On 04/01/26, echocardiography showed severe pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular strain. She remained oxygen-dependent at 2 L, with SpO₂ 91%, persistent tachycardia, raised JVP, and mild peripheral oedema. Oral furosemide 40 mg daily was started, with continued oxygen, breathing exercises, and mobilisation.

By 05–06/01/26, CTPA and echocardiography had confirmed CTEPH with severe pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular strain. Breathlessness was improving, oxygen saturation was 94% on 2 L, and sildenafil 20 mg three times daily was continued. Furosemide was monitored, and referral to a tertiary pulmonary hypertension centre for pulmonary endarterectomy assessment was planned. Physiotherapy progressed to corridor walking with rest breaks; saturations remained above 92%.

On 07/01/26, the V/Q scan showed mismatched perfusion defects consistent with CTEPH. She was less breathless, mobilising lightly, and maintained SpO₂ 95% on room air. Long-term anticoagulation with rivaroxaban 20 mg daily was initiated, with discharge planning and tertiary referral continued.

On 08/01/26, she reported reduced breathlessness and improved activity tolerance. Mild anaemia was documented with Hb 110 g/L, and ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily was started. Furosemide 20 mg daily was also prescribed for mild peripheral oedema. She participated well in breathing, energy-conservation, and mobility sessions.

On 09–10/01/26, she remained clinically stable with improving breathlessness, good mobilisation, clear lungs, no raised JVP or peripheral oedema, and SpO₂ 94% on room air. NT-proBNP remained elevated and Hb was 110 g/L. She was discharged on 10/01/26 with rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks followed by 20 mg daily, sildenafil 20 mg three times daily, and ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily. A home exercise programme, safety-netting advice, and follow-up at a tertiary pulmonary hypertension centre in approximately four weeks were arranged, with consideration of pulmonary endarterectomy.

43-year-old woman with hypertension and asthma, nut allergy, and no reported regular medications, presented on 03/01/26 with a 2-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness limiting daily activities. She denied chest pain, haemoptysis, fever, syncope, palpitations, or wheeze. Initial examination showed respiratory distress, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, raised JVP, basal crepitations, loud P2, and mild tender hepatomegaly without peripheral oedema. Oxygen saturation was 89–90% initially and improved to 92% on low-flow oxygen.

ABG showed mild hypoxia with respiratory alkalosis (PaO₂ 8.5 kPa, pH 7.46–7.47, low PaCO₂). NT-proBNP was markedly elevated (3,200–4,500 pg/mL), and D-dimer was elevated. Chest radiography showed pulmonary congestion/cardiomegaly without focal consolidation or pneumothorax. She was admitted to the Respiratory HDU with suspected chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and treated initially with therapeutic enoxaparin and supplemental oxygen.

CT pulmonary angiography confirmed chronic thromboembolic disease. Echocardiography demonstrated severe pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular strain. V/Q scanning subsequently showed mismatched perfusion defects, confirming the extent of CTEPH. There was no evidence of acute infection, and renal function remained stable. Cardiology and respiratory teams arranged referral to a tertiary pulmonary hypertension centre for pulmonary endarterectomy assessment.

Anticoagulation was transitioned during admission to apixaban and then rivaroxaban; the discharge regimen was rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days followed by 20 mg once daily. Sildenafil 20 mg three times daily was started for pulmonary hypertension. Furosemide was used during admission (40 mg once daily, later 20 mg once daily for mild oedema), and ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily was prescribed for mild anaemia (haemoglobin 110 g/L). Physiotherapy provided breathing exercises, mobilisation support, and a home exercise plan.

Her breathlessness and exercise tolerance progressively improved. Oxygen requirement decreased from 2 L/min to 1 L/min and she was subsequently stable on room air with saturations around 94–95%. By discharge on 10/01/26 she was mobilising independently, comfortable at rest, with clear chest, no raised JVP or peripheral oedema, and persistently elevated NT-proBNP. She was discharged on rivaroxaban, sildenafil, and ferrous sulfate, with tertiary pulmonary hypertension follow-up in four weeks, planned repeat haemoglobin and NT-proBNP, and advice to seek urgent care for worsening breathlessness or chest pain.
